extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students studying algebraic geometry (and researchers needing a concise reference)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and collects the key definitions, constructions, and exercise-guidance from a textbook chapter covering finitely generated graded rings, rational maps and birationality, representable functors and group schemes, and the Grassmannian. Useful for learners solving exercises or implementing the constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation in degree 1 (Veronese/regrading trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is generated in degree 1, show that S^{(n)} is also generated in degree 1. More generally, after regrading (keeping only terms of degree a multiple of d, then dividing degree by d) any finitely generated graded ring can be assumed to be generated in degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 7.4.G (hint): If generators x1,...,xn have degrees d1,...,dn, show that any monomial x1^{a1}...xn^{an} of sufficiently large degree has some ai ≥ (d1...dn)/di for some i; conclude the (nd1...dn)-th Veronese subring is generated in the "new" degree 1. Use this (and Exercise 7.4.D) to justify assuming finitely generated graded rings are generated in degree 1 after regrading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj invariance under finite-degree differences
rubrics_metrics.description: If R and S are finitely generated graded rings which differ only in a finite number of nonzero degrees, then Proj R and Proj S are the same (isomorphic) projective-type object. (Make the precise finite-degrees condition.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used together with regrading/Veronese tricks to show hypotheses about generation in degree 1 are harmless when studying Proj. The text suggests making precise which finite-degree differences are allowed and then checking Proj is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to finitely generated Veronese subrings
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists N (or a d) such that taking the N-th Veronese subring S^{(N)} yields a finitely generated graded ring generated in degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible approach: use Exercise 7.4.G-style bounds on monomial exponents; Exercise 7.4.H suggests choosing N so that S^{(N)} is finitely generated and then showing modules S^{(N)}_{+nj} are finitely generated over S^{(N)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rational map (reduced schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π of reduced schemes X →→ Y is the data of a morphism α: U → Y from a dense open subset U ⊂ X, considered up to the equivalence relation: (α:U→Y) ∼ (β:V→Y) if there exists a dense open Z ⊂ U ∩ V with α|Z = β|Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational maps need not be morphisms; the definition extends to S-schemes similarly. There is a notion of pseudo-morphism to control behavior on nonreduced loci (not used here). When Y is separated equivalence is easier to handle. People often misuse 'map' for 'morphism' — avoid ambiguity when meaning 'rational map'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant rational map
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π: X →→ Y is dominant if the image is dense in Y. This is independent of the representative: if a representative morphism α:U→Y has dense image then π is dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A morphism is called dominant if it is dominant as a rational map. Composition: composing a dominant rational map with another rational map produces a dominant composition when appropriate; dominant rational maps between integral schemes correspond contravariantly to inclusions of function fields in classical situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and category of dominant rational maps (integral schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant rational maps between integral schemes compose (in a well-defined way), and integral schemes with dominant rational maps form a category of geometric interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, ensure domains of representatives intersect appropriately. If the second map is dominant, the composition is dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birational map / birationality
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π: X →→ Y is birational if it is dominant and there exists a dominant rational inverse ψ: Y →→ X such that the compositions are the identity in the equivalence-class sense. A morphism is birational if it is birational as a rational map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Birationality is the notion of isomorphism in the category of integral schemes with dominant rational maps. In particular, birational maps induce isomorphisms of function fields; conversely, in integral finite type k-schemes a map inducing an isomorphism on function fields is birational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of birationality via isomorphic dense opens (Prop. 7.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced schemes X and Y are birational iff there exist dense open subschemes U ⊂ X and V ⊂ Y such that U ≅ V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof constructs representatives of the rational inverse maps and shrinks domains to produce the isomorphism on opens; the textbook provides a diagrammatic outline. This is the geometric intuition: birational schemes are 'mostly isomorphic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between dominant rational maps and function field inclusions (classical case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'suitably classical situations' (integral finite type k-schemes, e.g., irreducible varieties), dominant rational maps X →→ Y correspond contravariantly to inclusions of function fields K(Y) ↪ K(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: maps of function fields do not always give rational maps (example Spec k[x] vs Spec k(x)). Proposition 7.5.7 gives a construction: from an inclusion φ#: K(Y) → K(X) preserving k and after replacing Y by an open affine Spec B one produces a dominant rational map φ: X →→ Y inducing φ#.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domains of definition extend over regular codimension-one points (Curve-to-Projective Extension statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domains of definition of rational maps to projective schemes extend over regular codimension-one points; this is a recurring theme and is made precise in the Curve-to-Projective Extension Theorem 15.3.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (stereographic projection, Cremona transformation, conics) show how domains can be extended over many points but may fail over singular/codimension-one nonregular loci. The theorem is postponed to the curves section but is foreshadowed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps to A^1 correspond to global sections (functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection Mor(X, A^1) ≅ Γ(X, O_X) between maps from a scheme X to A^1 and global sections of the structure sheaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bijection is functorial in X (natural isomorphism of functors). Interpreting maps to A^1 as functions motivates representable functors and group schemes. The statement extends to rational maps: rational functions on an integral scheme can be interpreted as rational maps to A^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functor and uniqueness of representing object
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a category C (e.g., Sch), the contravariant functor h_Y(X)=Mor(X,Y) represents objects Y; a contravariant functor F: C→Sets is representable if F ≅ h_Y. If F is represented by Y and also by Z then Y ≅ Z uniquely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Yoneda-style perspective; Exercise 7.6.C and references to Yoneda's Lemma are given. Use this to recognize objects up to unique isomorphism via universal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard representability examples (A^n and G_m)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affine n-space A^n represents the functor assigning to X the n-tuple of functions (f1,...,fn) ∈ Γ(X,O_X)^n. The multiplicative group G_m = Spec Z[t,t^{-1}] represents the functor of invertible functions on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 7.6.E: demonstrate these universal properties. These examples motivate group schemes: G_m represents group-valued functor of invertible global functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and axioms of a group object (group scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group object in a category with final object Z and products is an object X with morphisms: multiplication m: X×X → X, inverse i: X → X, identity e: Z → X, satisfying categorical associativity, identity, and inverse axioms (commuting diagrams). A group scheme is a group object in the category of schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specializing to sets recovers ordinary groups. Exercises ask to give A^1_Z the structure of a group scheme (additive group: inverse t ↦ -t), check Mor(X,G) is a group for any X, and derive group morphisms functorially. Hopf algebra viewpoint for affine group schemes is mentioned as an aside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions and examples of group schemes (GL_n, SL_n, μ_n)
rubrics_metrics.description: GL_n can be made into a group scheme; det: GL_n → G_m is a morphism of group schemes and SL_n is its kernel (representable). The kernel of [·]^n on G_m (i.e., μ_n) is representable; over a field of characteristic p dividing n this group scheme is nonreduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises guide constructing GL_n as scheme of invertible n×n matrices, defining determinant map and checking kernels are representable and describe behavior in positive characteristic (nonreducedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Group scheme actions and gradings
rubrics_metrics.description: An action of a group scheme on a scheme is defined categorically. In particular, specifying an integer-valued grading on a ring A is equivalent to specifying an action of G_m on Spec A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 7.6.S notes two conventions for integer-valued gradings and cautions both are used in the literature. This interpretation illuminates gradings as symmetry data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassmannian construction by affine patches and gluing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Grassmannian G(k,n) is constructed by taking for each basis v of A^n an affine patch U_v ≅ A^{k(n-k)} with coordinates a_{ji} representing k-planes spanned by vectors v_i + sum_{j>k} a_{ji} v_j, and then gluing these patches along opens where certain determinants don't vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit construction shows the Grassmannian is covered by affine Schubert-type patches (open Schubert cell), yields dimension k(n-k) in classical geometry, and leads to further properties: Plücker embedding (projectivity) and GL_n action. Check triple intersections for consistency; later one shows G(k,n) is projective and has the Plücker embedding.
